passage: The judges announced the results of the Island Robotics Challenge in reverse order. Gus's robot, Clank, had been the favourite all week, and Gus had barely slept for a month getting it ready. He had even made Clank a tiny bow tie for the judging. When third place was called and it wasn't Clank, Gus smiled. When second place went to another team, he kept smiling. Then the winner was announced, and it was a robot called Duster, which mostly just swept the floor in neat little circles. Some people in the crowd gasped. The judges said Duster's design was simple, clever and very reliable. [Gus walked straight over and shook hands with Duster's builder.] 'Fair enough,' he said. 'Duster's very tidy.' [Then he asked her how Duster's sensors worked.] When Tully asked if he was okay, he said, 'Totally fine. Honestly. It's just a competition.' [The other teams cheered and crowded around Duster for photos.] [Gus packed Clank into its box without looking at anyone and slipped out before the photos.] [Duster's builder held the trophy high above her head.] Tully gave Mo a worried look. The crew didn't see Gus again until dinner, when he said he wasn't hungry, which had never happened before. Even Mo's famous sausage rolls stayed on the plate.

frame: Gus's robot butler is acting strangely. The Cubbler is hiding under the table.
text: Gus's robot butler, Jeeves, had been working perfectly all week. On Friday afternoon, though, things got weird. At lunch, Mo had been fiddling with the buttons on Jeeves's control panel, giggling to himself. He had pressed one marked PARTY MODE. At three o'clock, a little red battery light on Jeeves's back started flashing. Gus didn't notice, because he was busy in the lab. By four o'clock, Jeeves was rolling around the kitchen blasting loud music. Rainbow lights were flashing on his head. He was also moving slower and slower, and his arms had drooped until they hung limp by his sides. At five o'clock, he stopped in the middle of the floor. He didn't move again until Gus plugged him in.

passage: Log of the fishing boat Saltbush, Thursday. We left Hollowgum harbour at five o'clock this morning under a clear, pink sky, planning to fish the deep reef until sunset. The forecast the night before had promised light winds all day, and Loretta has fished these waters for thirty years. [By nine o'clock our nets were already half full of snapper, the best catch we'd had all month.] [Young Kip was seasick twice over the side, but he felt better after a ginger biscuit.] At half past nine, the radio crackled. [The weather bureau announced that a fierce southerly change would hit the coast by early afternoon, with winds of up to ninety kilometres an hour.] Captain Loretta listened carefully, then looked south, where a thin grey line had appeared along the horizon. She said nothing, but she pulled in the nets, turned the Saltbush around and pushed the engine as hard as it would go. [On the way back, a pod of dolphins rode our bow wave for almost a kilometre.] We tied up at the jetty at twenty past twelve. By one o'clock, the harbour was white with foam, and the masts of the moored boats were swinging like windscreen wipers. Captain Loretta poured herself a cup of tea and said, 'Snapper keeps.'

frame: Wren is making a Field Guide page about a creepy cave. It needs a heading.
text: Walk into Hollowgum Cave at night and switch off your torch. At first there is total darkness. Then, slowly, thousands of tiny blue lights appear on the roof, like a sky full of stars. It looks magical, but it is actually a deadly trap. Each light belongs to a glow-worm, which isn't really a worm at all but the larva of a small fly. The glow-worm hangs dozens of sticky threads, like fishing lines, from the cave roof. Flying insects head for the light, thinking it is the night sky, and get stuck. The glow-worm then reels the line in and eats its catch alive. Hungry glow-worms glow brighter. Visitors are asked to whisper, because loud noises can make the lights dim. Bats sleep near the entrance, so watch your head on the way in. Some people say the cave is haunted, but the only thing hunting in there is the glow-worms.

frame: The Gistling found a report from the reef station. Sort the big idea from the extras.
text: Most people walk straight past sea cucumbers. They look like soggy sausages lying on the sand, and they hardly move. They come in many colours, from plain brown to bright orange with blue spots. But without these lumpy creatures, coral reefs would be in serious trouble. A sea cucumber spends its day swallowing sand and digesting the tiny scraps of dead plants and animals in it. Then it poos out clean sand behind it. A single sea cucumber can clean dozens of kilograms of sand every year. Its droppings also release nutrients that help nearby coral and seagrass grow. Without them, waste would pile up on the sea floor, and the coral would struggle to grow. Sea cucumbers have some revolting habits, too. Many breathe through their bottoms. Some shoot out their own sticky guts to tangle attackers, then grow new ones. A small fish called a pearlfish sometimes lives inside a sea cucumber's bottom and pops out at night to feed. In some places, so many sea cucumbers have been collected that the sand around reefs has turned smelly and murky. Those murky reefs prove the point: a reef with no sea cucumbers is like a city where nobody takes out the rubbish.
